newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cites ice in Comair January crash near Detroit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cites ice in Comair January crash near Detroit.

text.p: Wing icing may have played a key role in the crash of a Comair commuter plane near Detroit last Jan. 9, along with the plane's performance and the training of its crew, investigators said on Wednesday,

They said there were widespread reports of ice in the area just before the plane went into a roll and plunged into the ground on its approach to Detroit Metropolitan Airport, killing all 29 people on board.
The National Transportation Safety Board said its reports were factual findings only and it had yet to analyse them and to make a determination of probable cause.
It is examining information that includes the flight data and cockpit recorders on the Embraer 120 Brasilia turboprop, regional weather reports and the plane's behaviour in icy weather conditions.
The board gave no indication when its investigation might be completed and a probable cause finding issued.

Flight and cockpit recorder data showed the plane, on a flight from Cincinnati on a connector link for Delta Air Lines Inc., proceeded without incident until 38 seconds before it went nose down into a snowy field.
Data from the flight recorder showed the Brazilian-built plane, made by Empresa Brasileira de Aeronautica, turning toward the right even though the autopilot tried to straighten out its flight.
Cockpit conversations with Detroit control showed the controller telling the Comair plane to turn left, and the pilot complying, but nothing after than.

There were several cockpit sounds, the board said, that could have been those that controls the plane's pitch, an increase in power, and that of a control stick shaking, which happens when wings lose lift.
The last sounds, the recorder showed, included a ground proximity warning that the plane was plunging toward earth.
Area weather reports showed some icing conditions, but flights into Detroit metropolitan were not disrupted, the investigators said.
But outside experts said the ice could have developed quickly on the Embraer's wings as it descended for a landing.
Following the crash of another commuter plane near Roselawn, Ind., in 1995, when icing was blamed, new training was developed to help pilots handle unsual attitudes encountered with icy wings.
The adequacy of training was being reviewed by the board, as well as the plane's performance in ice, the board said.
